sources.note: The complete Knowledge State schema (Assertions, Relationships, Evidence, History, Zero findings, Lord candidates) as a knowledge graph, later corrected to require Observer/Purpose/Context parameterization and to resolve a circularity from embedding Zero(K_t) and History inside K_t itself; paired with a System State that also includes the Ideal State and current inquiry.

rows.anchor: K_t \neq A Single Assertion ... K_t \neq A Set of Assertions ... K_t = A Structured Collection of Assertions + Their Relationships + Their Epistemic Status + Their History ... K_t = (A_t, R_t, E_t, H_t, Z_t, L_t)
rows.statement: Defines the Knowledge State K_t as a 6-component structure: Assertions A_t, Relationships R_t, Evidence E_t, History H_t (all previous Knowledge States), Zero findings Z_t, and Lord candidates L_t; forms a Knowledge Graph G_t=(A_t,R_t) with Assertions as nodes.

rows.anchor: Identical, Equivalent, Consistent, Contradictory, Causal, Temporal, Normative Conflict, Logical Contradiction ... R_j = (A_i, A_k, Type, Strength, Evidence)
rows.statement: Types the Relationship edges of the knowledge graph with eight relation kinds spanning both the earlier Compare vocabulary (Identical/Equivalent/Consistent/Contradictory) and the newer conflict taxonomy (Causal, Temporal, Normative Conflict, Logical Contradiction), each carrying Strength and supporting Evidence.

rows.anchor: State_t = (K_t, I_t, Q_t, C_t) ... I_t = (D_I, V_I, R_I, C_I) ... Compare(K_t, I_t) -> G_t
rows.statement: Introduces the complete System State as (KnowledgeState,IdealState,Question/Intent,Context), formalizes the Ideal State I_t=(IdealDimensions,IdealValues,IdealRelationships,Constraints), and defines Compare(K_t,I_t)->G_t as the set of gaps between current knowledge and the ideal.

rows.anchor: Zero Detection: Normative conflict between A_2 and A_3 ... Z_1 = (Normative Conflict, {A_2, A_3}, 'Family duty vs. war duty') ... Resolution... Zero Resolved: Z_1 is resolved.
rows.statement: Traces the full Arjuna example through five knowledge states K_0..K_4, showing a Zero-detected NormativeConflict finding created when the opposing-side assertion is added and resolved once the moral-conflict assertion clarifies the relation between the grandfather and opponent assertions as Compatible rather than contradictory.

rows.anchor: A Knowledge State should probably not be defined as 'everything KnowledgeOS has.' It should be defined as the epistemically structured state relevant to a particular observer, purpose, context and time... K_t = K(X,P,N,C,tau)
rows.statement: Rejects modelling K_t as an absolute, single global object; since the Observation model already parameterizes on Purpose/Observer/Context/Time, the Knowledge State must be similarly parameterized: K_t=K(X,Purpose,Knower,Context,tau), since two Knowers (Arjuna vs Dhrtarastra) observing the same reality do not share an identical Knowledge State.

type_signature.domain: Reality x Purpose x Knower x Context x Time

lineage_claims.quote: A Knowledge State should probably not be defined as 'everything KnowledgeOS has.'

rows.anchor: K_t \supset Z_t but Z_t=Zero(K_t) which means the state contains the output of an operation that operates on the state itself... I would therefore define: K_t = CurrentKnowledgeState and separately H_{0:t}=KnowledgeHistory
rows.statement: Flags a definitional circularity in the S0783 Knowledge State: embedding Z_t=Zero(K_t) and H_t={K_0,...,K_t} as components of K_t itself makes K_t contain the output of an operation applied to K_t, and makes each historical K_i recursively contain its own history; proposes separating CurrentKnowledgeState K_t from KnowledgeHistory H_{0:t} and computing Zero(K_t)/Lord(K_t) as derived views rather than stored fields.

rows.anchor: An assertion does not simply exist. It applies somewhere... Scope = (Context, Time, Subject, Boundary, ...) This is essential for avoiding false contradictions.
rows.statement: Introduces Scope as a missing concept an assertion needs (e.g. Nexus.Version=3.69 applies to production but not test; a policy applies to one organization but not another), motivated as necessary to avoid false apparent contradictions between assertions that actually hold in different scopes.

rows.anchor: Knowledge State \neq Conflict Free State ... Coherence = all assertions are mutually interpretable under their dimensions, scopes, contexts and temporal constraints ... A Knowledge State may contain unknowns, conflicts, competing interpretations, unresolved questions, normative tensions and still be coherent.
rows.statement: Redefines Coherence away from 'no contradictions' toward 'all assertions are mutually interpretable under their dimensions, scopes, contexts and temporal constraints', explicitly allowing a coherent Knowledge State to contain unknowns, unresolved normative tensions and competing interpretations without being incoherent -- Knowledge State != Conflict-Free State.
missing: formal Coherent(K_t) predicate, deferred to Question 7

rows.anchor: Question 13: What is the formal structure of the Knowledge State? ... Is Knowledge State a set, graph, typed graph, labelled graph, relational structure, lattice, or some composite algebraic structure?
rows.statement: Poses Question 13 as the prerequisite to formalizing distance: K_t must be given an exact formal structure (set/graph/typed-graph/relational-structure/lattice/composite) before any distance/measurement function over it can be mathematically meaningful.

rows.anchor: Knowledge State is the formal, typed, structured representation ... K_t = (A_t, R_t, E_t, H_t, Z_t, L_t, T_t, G_t, C_t, M_t) ... Knowledge State = A Structured Typed Graph with Epistemic Metadata
rows.statement: Proposes a ten-component Knowledge State (Assertions, Relationships, Evidence, History, ZeroFindings, LordCandidates, Temporal structure, Knowledge Graph, Context, Metadata/provenance) formalized as a typed, directed, labelled graph, with immutability of History (new states appended, never overwritten) as a core invariant.
invariants: New states are appended, never overwritten

rows.anchor: K contains things that are not knowledge ... Zero findings: No. Zero findings are observations about the Knowledge State. Lord candidates: Definitely no. History: Probably not part of the instantaneous Knowledge State. Knowledge Graph: probably a representation of the Knowledge State, not another independent component inside it.
rows.statement: Rejects the ten-component K_t as a category error: Zero findings and Lord candidates are derived observations/hypotheses about the state, not the state itself; History is a temporal model over states, not a field within one state; the typed graph is a representation/projection of the state, not an ontologically independent component. Proposes a smaller canonical K_t=(Propositions,Assertions,Relationships,Evidence,EpistemicState,Context,Temporal,Provenance) with Z_t=Zero(K_t,I_t,Q_t,C_t), L_t=Lord(K_t,I_t,Q_t,C_t), and H_t=History(K_0,...,K_t) all computed externally.

lineage_claims.quote: I would not accept this as the canonical Knowledge State.

rows.anchor: 'Contained in' is not the right mathematical relation. Entity not-subset Proposition ... use Participates In / Referenced By / Forms instead.
rows.statement: Corrects the typed-universe diagram's 'contained in' arrows (Entity/Dimension/Value -> Propositions) which are not subset relations: an entity participates in a proposition, a dimension is referenced by it; recommends participates-in/referenced-by/forms relations instead, consistent with the earlier containment-vs-set-inclusion correction from Question 7.

rows.anchor: SystemState_t = (K_t, U_t, X_t, I_t, Q_t, C_t, N_t, Z_t, L_t, H_t) ... K_t = Knowledge State only
rows.statement: Defines the complete runtime SystemState as wrapping the (now smaller) Knowledge State K_t together with Understanding U_t, Domain X_t, Ideal I_t, Intent/Question Q_t, Context C_t, Knower N_t, and the derived Z_t/L_t/H_t, cleanly separating what KnowledgeOS knows from what it also tracks about the Knower and the epistemic journey.

rows.anchor: Question 14 — What is the Ontology of Knowledge? Is a Proposition a value object? Is an Assertion an entity or value object? Is Evidence itself knowledge? Is a Relationship a proposition? Is an Epistemic State part of an assertion or external? Is a Gap part of knowledge or a finding about knowledge? Is Zero part of the domain model or an operation over it? Is the Knowledge Graph the ontology or merely one representation?
rows.statement: Poses Question 14 (Ontology of Knowledge) listing eight unresolved ontological-status questions (Proposition as value object? Assertion entity or value object? Evidence itself knowledge? Relationship a proposition? EpistemicState internal or external to Assertion? Gap knowledge or finding? Zero domain-model or operation? Graph ontology or representation?) to be resolved before implementation.

rows.anchor: There is no component of K holding the set of recognised dimensions. ... D_t is the smallest missing component. With it, 'not assessed' is D in D_t AND not exists a in A: a.P.D=D -- decidable in O(n). Without it, the statement has no truth-maker.
rows.statement: An executed probe (MISSINGNESS-NOT-ASSESSED in THEORY-CONSTRUCTION-TEST.md) shows a never-assessed dimension and an assessed-with-no-result dimension both render identically in K=(A,R) as 'no assertion mentioning that dimension', proving them provably indistinguishable; introducing D_t (the set of currently recognised dimensions) as a component of K makes 'not assessed' decidable in O(n) and is identified as the smallest missing component to close the missingness gap.

rows.anchor: A construction score is not a proof of adequacy. A scoring exercise establishes RELATIVE rank among the candidates enumerated; it establishes nothing about whether any candidate is sufficient, and it cannot detect a capability that NO candidate was scored on.
rows.statement: The claim that K=Set(Assertion) x R is correct because it scored highest (15/19) against six candidates is challenged on methodological grounds: a comparative score establishes only relative rank among enumerated candidates, never absolute sufficiency, and cannot detect capabilities no candidate was scored on -- exactly the three (uncertainty, non-identifiability, missingness) later shown to be missed.

rows.anchor: K is a representation whose referent is undeclared. That is why adequacy could only be argued by SCORING AGAINST CAPABILITIES, never by FIDELITY TO A REFERENT.
rows.statement: Testing five possible classifications of what K 'is' (ontology, mathematical state, representation, abstraction, domain-specific projection), only 'representation' is defensible, but its referent (the W it represents) is never named in the theory, so adequacy can currently only be judged by capability-scoring rather than fidelity to a declared referent; once Omega:W->O exists, adequacy becomes answerable, but not before.
missing: a declared referent W for K

rows.anchor: Three of eleven have no body: dedup (does not exist), Sigma's strength rule, delta's commit case.
rows.statement: A table of eleven operations over K (member, add, merge, supersede, contradicts, dedup, Sigma, Gamma, delta, History, Lineage) with signatures, preconditions, postconditions, determinism and failure modes shows three have no defined body: dedup does not exist as an operation, Sigma's strength rule is absent, and delta's body is undefined for the commit case.

rows.anchor: id before withdrawal : 86a0330e2b65 / id after withdrawal : a9d84e7a43d8 / SAME? False / R edge (...) now dangles: True ... The theory's identity rule and its mutability rule cannot both hold.
rows.statement: Executing kaudit.py shows that because id is declared derived as H(P,e,c,t,Pi) while e.state is declared mutable, withdrawing one evidence item re-keys the assertion's id and breaks every R edge pointing at the old id, violating StructuralValid's own no-dangling clause -- an internal contradiction between the identity rule and the mutability rule in the same field table, worsened by the audit's own addition of a mutable state field to e.

lineage_claims.target: the audit's section 7 amendment adding state to e
lineage_claims.quote: the audit's section 7 amendment that added state to e created this contradiction

experiment.hypothesis: id=H(P,e,c,t,Pi) is stable under a declared-mutable e.state field.
experiment.setup: construct an assertion, compute its id, mutate e.state via withdrawal, recompute id
experiment.assumptions: id is derived by hashing the full field tuple including e
experiment.inputs: a single assertion with one evidence item
experiment.method: compare id before/after withdrawal and check whether existing R edges still resolve
experiment.result: ids differ (86a0330e2b65 vs a9d84e7a43d8); the R edge referencing the old id now dangles
experiment.interpretation: identity and mutability rules are jointly inconsistent
experiment.limitations: single executed example, but the contradiction is structural not incidental
experiment.conclusion: REFUTED: the theory's identity rule and its mutability rule cannot both hold

rows.anchor: Because Pi is inside id, the same fact from two sources is two assertions. ... K grows without bound under re-observation ... R is not maintained by merge.
rows.statement: Executing kaudit.py shows two assertions of the identical proposition from two different sources get distinct ids (because Pi/provenance is inside id), so merge-as-union cannot deduplicate: corroboration becomes indistinguishable from duplication, K grows unboundedly under repeated observation of the same fact, merge's idempotence holds only for byte-identical assertions, and cross-state relations between semantic twins are never created by merge, silently dropping information.
missing: a dedup operator on (P,c,t) unioning Pi and e

experiment.hypothesis: merge=union is an adequate deduplication operation for K.
experiment.setup: construct two assertions of the same proposition P with two different sources
experiment.assumptions: Pi (provenance) is a field inside the assertion id hash
experiment.inputs: two Assertion objects with identical P but distinct Provenance
experiment.method: compute both ids and compare
experiment.result: ids differ (86a0330e2b65 vs f847660b1940)
experiment.interpretation: the same fact from two sources produces two distinct assertions under merge=union
experiment.limitations: single executed pair, but the mechanism (Pi inside id) generalizes
experiment.conclusion: REFUTED as adequate: merge=union cannot deduplicate

rows.anchor: Two assertions joined by an explicit contradicts edge are both Supporting. Sigma ... has no access to R by its own signature. ... R and Sigma are two independent accounts of epistemic force that are never reconciled.
rows.statement: A new finding (not on the prior audit's 12-attack list): executing kaudit.py shows two assertions joined by an explicit 'contradicts' relation in R both receive Sigma=(Supporting,Weak), because Sigma:Assertion x Policy -> (dir,str) has no access to R by its own signature, so K can hold a fully-supported inconsistency unless a policy gate independently re-derives contradiction.

experiment.hypothesis: Sigma reflects contradictions recorded in R.
experiment.setup: two assertions c1,c2 joined by an explicit contradicts edge in R
experiment.assumptions: Sigma is computed per-assertion from Policy alone, as declared
experiment.inputs: c1,c2 with a contradicts relation between them
experiment.method: compute Sigma(c1) and Sigma(c2) and compare to the presence of the contradicts edge
experiment.result: both Sigma(c1) and Sigma(c2) = (Supporting, Weak)
experiment.interpretation: R and Sigma are disconnected accounts of epistemic force
experiment.limitations: single executed pair
experiment.conclusion: NEW FINDING: contradiction is invisible to epistemic status absent a policy re-derivation

rows.anchor: Gamma : Assertion x GovCtx -> {Uncommitted, Committed, ...} is derived and is NOT a component of K. delta(K, e) must therefore record a commitment somewhere in A or R, and neither has a carrier. The system's central act -- crossing the decision boundary -- has no state transition.
rows.statement: Executing kaudit.py's commit sequence shows K1 is K0 (True) after a commit event: since Gamma (commitment status) is derived rather than stored as a component of K, delta has nowhere in A or R to record a commitment, so the theory's central act -- crossing the decision boundary -- produces no state transition at all; this is the direct structural cost of storing Gamma nowhere, mirroring in reverse the audit's own observation that storing status caused update anomalies in other candidates.
missing: a carrier in A or R for commitment status

lineage_claims.target: the audit's scoring of candidates E and F for storing status
lineage_claims.quote: The scoring recorded the cost of storing and NOT the cost of not storing, which is that delta becomes undefined.

experiment.hypothesis: delta(K,e) produces a state change when e is a commit event.
experiment.setup: construct a command c_t={'cmd':'commit',...}, an event e_t={'event':'Committed',...}, apply delta
experiment.assumptions: Gamma is computed from K rather than stored in it
experiment.method: apply delta(K0, e_t) to get K1 and compare K1 to K0
experiment.result: K1 is K0: True (no change)
experiment.interpretation: the commit produces no observable state transition
experiment.limitations: single executed example
experiment.conclusion: REFUTED: the central commit act has no state transition in the current shape of K

rows.anchor: GovernanceValid requires History; History is not a function of K; therefore GovernanceValid is not a predicate over the declared state space. Two K-equal states can differ in governance validity.
rows.statement: Answering the mandate's equality questions: identical assertions with different histories are K-equal (History is external to K, per an executed probe), but identical assertions with different provenance are NOT K-equal (Pi is inside id); consequently GovernanceValid, which requires History, is not a predicate over K's declared state space -- the canonical theory calls this 'a boundary, not a defect', but it is argued here to be a typing defect: one of four declared validity predicates is undefined on the space it is declared over.

lineage_claims.target: the canonical theory's characterization of this as 'a boundary, not a defect'
lineage_claims.quote: which is a defect in the typing, whatever it is in the architecture

rows.anchor: 8 of 13 hold, 2 are defective, 3 are absent.
rows.statement: A scorecard of thirteen tested capabilities of K=(A,R) finds identity inconsistent with mutability, merge union-only with no dedup and lost cross-state relations, and contradiction invisible to Sigma (all defective); deduplication, unknown-bottom-element, missingness and non-identifiability are entirely absent; equality, membership, supersession, temporal evolution, provenance and evidence association hold -- totalling 8 held, 2 defective, 3 absent.

rows.anchor: VERIFIER RECOMMENDS -- not CORPUS ESTABLISHES. K = (D_t, A, R) ... with id = H(P, e_refs, c, t, Pi) where e_refs projects out the mutable state. ... Nothing here is adopted. This is a proposal, and it is smaller than the three the corpus already contains -- which should be consumed first (ES-005.4).
rows.statement: Proposes (explicitly labelled VERIFIER RECOMMENDS, not adopted) a minimal repair K=(D_t,A,R) adding the recognised-dimension set D_t and redefining id=H(P,e_refs,c,t,Pi) to project out the mutable state field, arguing this closes the missingness gap (7/8 cases), removes the identity/mutability contradiction, and makes a dedup operator definable by unioning Pi and e on (P,c,t); explicitly states this does not repair non-identifiability (needs a W,Omega layer beneath K) or uncertainty (needs U(H)), and that the corpus's own existing three constructions should be consumed first per ES-005.4.

rows.anchor: K = (A, R) as a shape: EXECUTED (40 assertions, 59 typed relations, live). K = (A,R) as minimal/sufficient: UNRESOLVED
rows.statement: The reconstruction's honest scorecard rates K=(A,R) as EXECUTED as a shape (via the EKP instantiation) but UNRESOLVED as a minimality or sufficiency claim, since EXP-3 (referenced) shows the answer depends on an operation set the corpus never closes; likewise Sigma_lifecycle-perp-Sigma_source-trust is IMPLEMENTED+EMPIRICALLY OBSERVED while Sigma_epistemic is UNRESOLVED/absent from the implementation entirely, and any quantitative epistemic measure is REFUTED as a measurement (mean-over-ladder flips, AggregateSupport unbounded/non-idempotent, IndependenceFactor conflates depth with independence, confidence not a probability without a declared (Omega,F,P)).

rows.anchor: Eleven of fifteen mandated objects were built. Three (unknown, uncertainty, missingness) could not be represented at all; one (authorization) required inventing a function body; and the transformation that ties them together is a no-op for its central case. ... Eight such points were reached.
rows.statement: Constructing the smallest complete KnowledgeOS instance strictly from the canonical theory succeeds for 11 of 15 mandated objects (two assertions, evidence, provenance, temporal validity, contradiction, policy, assessment Sigma, verdict Apply, history, lineage, and a transformation pipeline that runs but is a no-op), fails to represent unknown/uncertainty/missingness at all, and requires inventing a function body for authorization; per the mandate's own rule, each point requiring an invented definition counts as a theory gap, and eight such points were reached.

assumptions.statement: a required object that cannot be constructed without inventing a definition is a theory gap
assumptions.anchor: Per mandate §14: 'If any required object cannot be constructed without inventing a definition, that is a theory gap.'

experiment.hypothesis: the canonical theory as amended by THEORY-CLOSURE-AUDIT.md is sufficient to construct the smallest complete KnowledgeOS instance.
experiment.setup: executed scripts construct.py and kaudit.py building two assertions, evidence, provenance, temporal validity, contradiction, policy, assessment, verdict, history, lineage, transformation, and authorization
experiment.assumptions: only definitions actually present in the canonical theory may be used; any invented content must be recorded as a gap
experiment.method: attempt construction of each object in pipeline order, halting and recording a gap wherever a definition had to be invented
experiment.result: 11/15 built (2 with caveats: transformation no-op, authorization invented body), 3 unbuildable (unknown, uncertainty, missingness), 8 distinct gap points recorded
experiment.interpretation: the theory's central governed transition and three core epistemic representations cannot be executed as specified
experiment.limitations: one instance, hand-constructed
experiment.conclusion: CONSTRUCTION INCOMPLETE

rows.anchor: Sigma(A1)=Sigma(A2)=('Supporting','Weak') while (A1, A2, contradicts) in R. Two assertions in an explicit contradiction edge both read as supported. Sigma's signature gives it no access to R.
rows.statement: In the constructed instance, two assertions joined by an explicit 'contradicts' relation edge both receive Sigma=(Supporting,Weak), confirming (cross-referenced to KNOWLEDGE-STATE-FINAL-AUDIT.md §3.3) that Sigma's signature has no access to R and so cannot reflect recorded contradictions.

lineage_claims.quote: Full analysis: KNOWLEDGE-STATE-FINAL-AUDIT.md §3.3.

rows.anchor: FIRST STOP -- qualification, at step 3 of 15. ... SECOND STOP -- K_{t+1}, at step 12 of 15. ... The pipeline is executable end-to-end only if an author supplies the qualification step by hand and accepts that the commit is a no-op. ... It does not hold for commit, which is the operation the theory is about.
rows.statement: Walking the mandated 15-step pipeline (input->observation->qualification->evidence->assertion->K_t->policy evaluation->authorization->command->execution->event->K_t+1->assessment->verdict->lineage) in order, execution first becomes impossible at step 3 (qualification, Qualify:Observation x Policy -> Evidence has no body) and again at step 12 (K_t+1, delta cannot write the commit); this directly contradicts a prior audit claim (§18) that K1=delta(K0,e0) was executed end-to-end and independently implementable -- that claim is shown to hold only for non-governance operations, not for commit, the operation the theory is centrally about.

lineage_claims.quote: holds only for non-governance operations. It does not hold for commit, which is the operation the theory is about.

rows.anchor: Result: 18 PASS . 3 PASS-with-defect . 9 FAIL. Two further symbols required by the corpus are NOT in the audit's list at all and would be additional failures: I (the inferential procedure E_q --I--> Q, 230.15) and N (the Knower space).
rows.statement: An independent re-audit of 30 core symbols (entity space, dimension space, value space, Time, Provenance, Proposition, Assertion, id-hash, Evidence, Observation, Qualify, Sufficient, K, R, member, structural/semantic equality, merge, dedup, contradicts, Sigma, Gamma, Policy, Apply/Gate, Assessment, Auth/Authority, Authorize, delta, History/Lineage) against a strict PASS-only-with-a-decision-procedure standard finds 18 PASS, 3 PASS-with-defect (Assertion/id hashing mutable state; merge inadequate for dedup; Gamma derived and uncomputable from K alone), and 9 FAIL (Observation, Qualify, Sufficient, dedup, Sigma's str rule, Assessment, Authority, Authorize, delta); identifies two further symbols required by the corpus but entirely absent from the audit's list -- the inferential procedure I (230.15) and N the Knower space -- as additional failures.

assumptions.statement: a symbol is PASS only if a decision procedure exists; prose does not qualify; a parameterised symbol is COMPUTABLE-AFTER-BINDING, never computable

rows.anchor: Six missing edges. Four of them lie on the single path from a human decision to a knowledge-state change -- the path the whole architecture exists to govern.
rows.statement: Walking the dependency chain Primitive->Definition->Derived object->Operation->Invariant->Policy->Authority->Execution->Observation->Evidence->Knowledge state->Assessment->Verdict->History/Lineage identifies six missing edges: World->Observation (no W, no Omega), Observation->Evidence (Qualify has no body), AuthorityAct->Command (no act object), Command->Event (Event has no schema), Event->Gamma (delta cannot write governance status), and R->Sigma (Sigma cannot see contradiction); four of the six lie consecutively on the single path from a human decision to a knowledge-state change, the path the architecture exists to govern.

rows.anchor: nodes whose definition transitively reaches a class-C object: 11/26 ... the central object K is itself in the blocked set, and so are T, ==, K* and History. Step 266's own candidate principle ... is stated but never applied to the graph.
rows.statement: Finding ON-2: propagating Step 266's class-C (no-decision-procedure) set through the dependency graph via its own stated principle Computability(T) => Computability(all semantic dependencies of T) -- which Step 266 states but never applies -- blocks 11 of 26 nodes including K, T (transformation), the congruence relation, K*, and History; the ten unblocked (computable) nodes are Context, Dimension, Entity, Observation, Proposition, Provenance, RelationType, Source, Time, Value. This sharpens Step 266 §266.34's 'K* is still not proven' into: K as currently defined cannot be computable, because Assertion carries an evidence field whose relation depends on a relevance predicate with no decision procedure.
invariants: Computability(T) => Computability(all semantic dependencies of T)

lineage_claims.quote: This is not a contradiction of Step 266; it is its unstated consequence.

rows.anchor: Split the assertion: A_struct = (id, P, c, t, Pi) and A = A_struct + e + sigma. A_struct depends only on unblocked nodes, so K_struct = (A_struct, R) IS in the computable core -- and it is exactly the object the EKP already runs. ... This session offers it as PROPOSED, not as a finding.
rows.statement: Proposes (labelled PROPOSED, not a finding) splitting Assertion into a structural part A_struct=(id,P,c,t,Pi), depending only on computable nodes, plus an evidence/status qualification layer (e,sigma) that crosses Step 266 §266.31's named judgement boundary; K_struct=(A_struct,R) would then lie in the computable core and is claimed to be exactly the object the EKP already runs (40 cards, 59 edges).

rows.anchor: id = H(P, {e.ref}, c, t, Pi) -- project out the mutable e.state. Evidence state then belongs to the assertion's mutable projection, not its identity. Smallest possible change; removes a contradiction rather than adding a concept.
rows.statement: Proposes (VERIFIER RECOMMENDS, TG-06) redefining id=H(P,{e.ref},c,t,Pi), projecting out the mutable e.state field, to resolve the identity/mutability contradiction (TG-06) with the smallest possible change -- removing a contradiction rather than adding a new concept -- consistent with the same minimal repair proposed independently in KNOWLEDGE-STATE-FINAL-AUDIT.md.

lineage_claims.quote: the smallest possible change

rows.anchor: Step 265's verdict -- provenance goes INSIDE the assertion -- is widely cited as what makes the state sufficient. It is NOT. The load-bearing component is R_der. Step 265's placement decision is ORTHOGONAL to the sufficiency question and should stop being cited for it.
rows.statement: Finding KG-3 (EXP-2): constructs two knowledge states holding the same propositions with the same per-proposition provenance, differing only in the presence of a 'derives' relation, and shows they diverge under withdraw() (one becomes empty, the other retains a derived proposition), demonstrating that provenance-in-assertion (Step 265's placement decision) is NOT what makes the state sufficient -- the load-bearing component is R_der -- so Step 265's placement should stop being cited as a sufficiency argument.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 265's placement decision is orthogonal to the sufficiency question and should stop being cited for it.

experiment.hypothesis: placing provenance inside the assertion is what makes K=(A,R) a sufficient state representation.
experiment.setup: two states KA, KB with the same propositions and same per-proposition provenance, KA lacking and KB having a 'derives' relation
experiment.assumptions: withdraw() is a legitimate operation whose effect distinguishes sufficient from insufficient representations
experiment.method: apply withdraw('vendor') to both and compare resulting proposition sets
experiment.result: KA becomes empty; KB retains Nexus.version=3.69 (derived)
experiment.interpretation: the relation set R_der, not provenance placement, is what preserves the distinction
experiment.limitations: single constructed pair
experiment.conclusion: REFUTED: content+in-assertion-provenance is not sufficient; the counterexample is withdraw

rows.anchor: id before withdrawal : ... id after withdrawal : ... SAME? ... => the canonical field table declares e.state MUTABLE and id DERIVED from e. Mutating state re-keys the assertion and breaks every R edge into it, violating StructuralValid's own 'no dangling' clause. CONTRADICTION.
rows.statement: Reproduces, as directly runnable source code, the four KNOWLEDGE-STATE-FINAL-AUDIT.md probes: PROBE 1 shows withdrawing evidence changes an assertion's content-addressed id and dangles a relation edge pointing at the old id; PROBE 2 shows the same proposition from two sources yields two distinct ids under merge=union; PROBE 3 shows Sigma computed independently of R gives two contradicting assertions the identical 'Supporting/Weak' status; PROBE 4 shows two K states built via different histories (import-only vs import-add-remove) compare equal, since History is external to K.

lineage_claims.quote: KNOWLEDGE-STATE-FINAL-AUDIT executable probes against K=(A,R), id=H(P,e,c,t,Pi).

rows.anchor: OBJECTS THAT COULD NOT BE CONSTRUCTED WITHOUT INVENTING A DEFINITION ... [1] UNKNOWN-VALUE ... [8] DELTA-COMMIT-SEMANTICS
rows.statement: Reproduces, as directly runnable source code, THEORY-CONSTRUCTION-TEST.md's construction of the smallest complete KnowledgeOS instance, tagging each of eight points (UNKNOWN-VALUE, MISSINGNESS-NOT-ASSESSED, UNCERTAINTY, NON-IDENTIFIABILITY, SARATHI-BODY, AUTHORIZE-BODY, KNOWER-SPACE-N, DELTA-COMMIT-SEMANTICS) where a definition had to be invented via an explicit invent(tag,why) call rather than silently supplied.

rows.anchor: P != A (Step 262). ... Admission is not a truth function (Closure-03). ... this is the single most important semantic decision in the whole corpus. ... Evidence is a relation, not a substance (Closure-04).
rows.statement: Restates and endorses (CORPUS ESTABLISHES) three genuine semantic achievements to be preserved by any successor theory: (1) P != A -- a proposition is timeless/contextless/sourceless, an assertion is that content placed by someone somewhere at some time with some backing, so two assertions of the same proposition are two objects (Step 262); (2) admission is not a truth function (Closure-03) -- an assertion enters K via a governed admission rule, not because it is true, so K can and must contain refuted assertions to explain how it came to be wrong, called the single most important semantic decision in the whole corpus; (3) Evidence is a relation not a substance (Closure-04), argued via the 3.69/secure/secure-for-five-years counterexample.

rows.anchor: | **Knowledge State** | `20260821` complex-numbers-in-knowledgeos-modeling | **247** | **596** | **most unstable object in the corpus** |
rows.statement: A whole-corpus definitional scan across 34 concepts and 1,555 files finds Knowledge State the single most dispersed/unstable object in the corpus (247 files, 596 distinct right-hand-side definitions), followed by Evidence (184 files, 299 distinct RHS, the highest dispersion), Verdict (112) and Observation (146); three concepts load-bearing in the claimed theory are correspondingly thin: ValueSpace (5 files), Sufficiency (5), TemporalValidity (3).

CONCEPTS = ["Assertion","Proposition","Observation","Evidence","Dimension","ValueSpace","Value",
 "KnowledgeState",...]
rows.statement: The concept-ledger tool scans 32 named concepts (Assertion, Proposition, Observation, Evidence, KnowledgeState, Relation, Policy, Authority, EpistemicStatus, GovernanceStatus, Sufficiency, Admissibility, Verdict, AuthorityAct, Zero, TemporalValidity, etc.) across the whole corpus excluding the verification/ tree, matching definitional patterns (`X := ...`, `X = ...`, `X ≡ ...`), sorted by filename timestamp, and reports first-appearance file, file count, and distinct-RHS count per concept as an upper-bound dispersion signal.

Six candidate state abstractions are implemented for comparative congruence testing: F1 content-only, F2 content+status, F3 id+content+status, F4 K=(A,R) [marked TERMINAL, i.e. the claimed/ratified model], F5 K=(A,R)+merge-source, and F6 full-state [control].

This is a proposal, and it is smaller than the three the corpus already contains -- which should be consumed first (ES-005.4).

rationale_evidence.anchor: There is no component of K holding the set of recognised dimensions. ... D_t is the smallest missing component. With it, 'not assessed' is D in D_t AND not exists a in A: a.P.D=D -- decidable in O(n). Without it, the statement has no truth-maker.
rationale_evidence.statement: An executed probe (MISSINGNESS-NOT-ASSESSED in THEORY-CONSTRUCTION-TEST.md) shows a never-assessed dimension and an assessed-with-no-result dimension both render identically in K=(A,R) as 'no assertion mentioning that dimension', proving them provably indistinguishable; introducing D_t (the set of currently recognised dimensions) as a component of K makes 'not assessed' decidable in O(n) and is identified as the smallest missing component to close the missingness gap.

rationale_evidence.anchor: A construction score is not a proof of adequacy. A scoring exercise establishes RELATIVE rank among the candidates enumerated; it establishes nothing about whether any candidate is sufficient, and it cannot detect a capability that NO candidate was scored on.
rationale_evidence.statement: The claim that K=Set(Assertion) x R is correct because it scored highest (15/19) against six candidates is challenged on methodological grounds: a comparative score establishes only relative rank among enumerated candidates, never absolute sufficiency, and cannot detect capabilities no candidate was scored on -- exactly the three (uncertainty, non-identifiability, missingness) later shown to be missed.

rationale_evidence.anchor: K is a representation whose referent is undeclared. That is why adequacy could only be argued by SCORING AGAINST CAPABILITIES, never by FIDELITY TO A REFERENT.
rationale_evidence.statement: Testing five possible classifications of what K 'is' (ontology, mathematical state, representation, abstraction, domain-specific projection), only 'representation' is defensible, but its referent (the W it represents) is never named in the theory, so adequacy can currently only be judged by capability-scoring rather than fidelity to a declared referent; once Omega:W->O exists, adequacy becomes answerable, but not before.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Three of eleven have no body: dedup (does not exist), Sigma's strength rule, delta's commit case.
rationale_evidence.statement: A table of eleven operations over K (member, add, merge, supersede, contradicts, dedup, Sigma, Gamma, delta, History, Lineage) with signatures, preconditions, postconditions, determinism and failure modes shows three have no defined body: dedup does not exist as an operation, Sigma's strength rule is absent, and delta's body is undefined for the commit case.

rationale_evidence.anchor: GovernanceValid requires History; History is not a function of K; therefore GovernanceValid is not a predicate over the declared state space. Two K-equal states can differ in governance validity.
rationale_evidence.statement: Answering the mandate's equality questions: identical assertions with different histories are K-equal (History is external to K, per an executed probe), but identical assertions with different provenance are NOT K-equal (Pi is inside id); consequently GovernanceValid, which requires History, is not a predicate over K's declared state space -- the canonical theory calls this 'a boundary, not a defect', but it is argued here to be a typing defect: one of four declared validity predicates is undefined on the space it is declared over.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 8 of 13 hold, 2 are defective, 3 are absent.
rationale_evidence.statement: A scorecard of thirteen tested capabilities of K=(A,R) finds identity inconsistent with mutability, merge union-only with no dedup and lost cross-state relations, and contradiction invisible to Sigma (all defective); deduplication, unknown-bottom-element, missingness and non-identifiability are entirely absent; equality, membership, supersession, temporal evolution, provenance and evidence association hold -- totalling 8 held, 2 defective, 3 absent.

rationale_evidence.anchor: FIRST STOP -- qualification, at step 3 of 15. ... SECOND STOP -- K_{t+1}, at step 12 of 15. ... The pipeline is executable end-to-end only if an author supplies the qualification step by hand and accepts that the commit is a no-op. ... It does not hold for commit, which is the operation the theory is about.
rationale_evidence.statement: Walking the mandated 15-step pipeline (input->observation->qualification->evidence->assertion->K_t->policy evaluation->authorization->command->execution->event->K_t+1->assessment->verdict->lineage) in order, execution first becomes impossible at step 3 (qualification, Qualify:Observation x Policy -> Evidence has no body) and again at step 12 (K_t+1, delta cannot write the commit); this directly contradicts a prior audit claim (§18) that K1=delta(K0,e0) was executed end-to-end and independently implementable -- that claim is shown to hold only for non-governance operations, not for commit, the operation the theory is centrally about.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Result: 18 PASS . 3 PASS-with-defect . 9 FAIL. Two further symbols required by the corpus are NOT in the audit's list at all and would be additional failures: I (the inferential procedure E_q --I--> Q, 230.15) and N (the Knower space).
rationale_evidence.statement: An independent re-audit of 30 core symbols (entity space, dimension space, value space, Time, Provenance, Proposition, Assertion, id-hash, Evidence, Observation, Qualify, Sufficient, K, R, member, structural/semantic equality, merge, dedup, contradicts, Sigma, Gamma, Policy, Apply/Gate, Assessment, Auth/Authority, Authorize, delta, History/Lineage) against a strict PASS-only-with-a-decision-procedure standard finds 18 PASS, 3 PASS-with-defect (Assertion/id hashing mutable state; merge inadequate for dedup; Gamma derived and uncomputable from K alone), and 9 FAIL (Observation, Qualify, Sufficient, dedup, Sigma's str rule, Assessment, Authority, Authorize, delta); identifies two further symbols required by the corpus but entirely absent from the audit's list -- the inferential procedure I (230.15) and N the Knower space -- as additional failures.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Six missing edges. Four of them lie on the single path from a human decision to a knowledge-state change -- the path the whole architecture exists to govern.
rationale_evidence.statement: Walking the dependency chain Primitive->Definition->Derived object->Operation->Invariant->Policy->Authority->Execution->Observation->Evidence->Knowledge state->Assessment->Verdict->History/Lineage identifies six missing edges: World->Observation (no W, no Omega), Observation->Evidence (Qualify has no body), AuthorityAct->Command (no act object), Command->Event (Event has no schema), Event->Gamma (delta cannot write governance status), and R->Sigma (Sigma cannot see contradiction); four of the six lie consecutively on the single path from a human decision to a knowledge-state change, the path the architecture exists to govern.

assumption_register.anchor: Per mandate §14: 'If any required object cannot be constructed without inventing a definition, that is a theory gap.'

sources.note: Step 246's four-part stress test (identity/equality/contradiction/uncertainty) of the Step-245 K0 candidate; converges on a Knowledge Substrate + Semantic Relations + Epistemic Qualifications + Regime-Specific-Projections decomposition with a Projection_R:K x R->Y_R interface and an identity-preservation invariant, corrects the assumed G1->G2->G3 dependency chain, and leaves provenance minimality and Knowledge-State equality explicitly open.

rows.anchor: They may support the same proposition p=HasVersion(S,v1) while remaining distinct evidence objects. Therefore we need at least three relations: Identity, Equality, Support. These must not be conflated.
rows.statement: Establishes via a two-observation example (o1 by System A at t1, o2 by System B at t2, both supporting the same proposition p) that Identity, Equality, and Support must be three distinct, non-conflatable relations: distinct observations can support the same proposition without being identical or equal to each other.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS may require domain identity in addition to mathematical equality ... a possible distinction is: StructuralEqual(x,y) versus SameIdentity(x,y). This is not yet an accepted KnowledgeOS definition. It is a required question.
rows.statement: Poses object-level StructuralEqual(x,y) versus SameIdentity(x,y) as a required, not-yet-answered distinction: two records may be structurally identical while referring to different historical occurrences, so domain identity may be needed beyond ordinary mathematical equality.

rows.anchor: There are at least four possibilities. A. Syntactic equality ... B. Semantic equality ... C. Observational equality ... D. Provenance-sensitive equality ... These are not interchangeable.
rows.statement: Defines four non-interchangeable candidate Knowledge-State equality relations: syntactic (byte/structural identity), semantic (same knowledge semantics), observational (same result under every permitted observation), and provenance-sensitive (content and relevant provenance equivalent).

rows.anchor: K1={p,e1} and K2={p,e2} where e1!=e2 but Supports(e1,p) and Supports(e2,p). Should K1=K2? There is no obvious answer. ... This proves that equality cannot be defined until we know what constitutes semantically essential information. Equality depends on the ontology and semantics.
rows.statement: Gives a worked counterexample (two states differing only in which distinct evidence item supports the same proposition) showing equality is undecidable until it is settled whether provenance is semantically constitutive of knowledge identity or merely metadata -- concluding equality is ontology/semantics-dependent, not free-standing.

rows.anchor: The mandate explicitly tells us not to assume this dependency ordering [G1->G2->G3]. ... the dependency graph is more accurately: Ontology -> State Representation -> Semantic Identity -> Equality ... So G1->G3 is plausible, but G1->G2->G3 is not established.
rows.statement: Corrects a previously assumed linear dependency ordering (G1: what is a KnowledgeState -> G2: what is epistemic status -> G3: what is equality) into a revised chain Ontology -> State Representation -> Semantic Identity -> Equality, with epistemic status interacting with both representation and equality rather than sitting strictly between state-definition and equality; the direct G1->G2->G3 chain is explicitly downgraded to not established.

rows.anchor: The propositions may refer to different times ... Then there is no contradiction. This demonstrates that contradiction cannot be determined from proposition content alone. ... A better candidate is: Contradicts(p1,p2,c) ... contradiction is likely a derived semantic relation, not a primitive field o
rows.statement: Shows via a temporal-interval example (HasVersion(S,v1) valid on [t1,t2), HasVersion(S,v2) valid on [t2,t3)) that two propositions with conflicting content are not automatically contradictory, since contradiction depends on context c as well as content; concludes contradiction is a derived semantic relation Contradicts(p1,p2,c), not a primitive Knowledge-State field.

rows.anchor: with both assert validity over exactly the same interval ... If the domain invariant is: forall t: #Version(S,t)<=1, then Contradicts(p1,p2)=true. ... Contradiction required: proposition semantics; temporal validity; domain constraints. Contradiction is not merely a property of two strings.
rows.statement: Gives a strong-contradiction example: two version propositions over the identical time interval, evaluated against an explicit domain invariant (a service has at most one version at any time) actually do produce Contradicts=true, demonstrating contradiction requires jointly proposition semantics, temporal validity, and domain constraints -- it is a relation evaluated under a semantic regime, not a syntactic property.

rows.anchor: A logical regime could define Contradiction_L. A temporal regime could define Contradiction_T. A probabilistic regime might instead calculate P(p1|E) and P(p2|E). These need not produce the same classification. Contradiction may be regime-relative.
rows.statement: Proposes that contradiction may be regime-relative: a logical regime, a temporal regime, and a probabilistic regime applied to the same pair of propositions need not agree on whether a contradiction exists -- a stronger claim than merely 'KnowledgeOS supports contradictions', and supportive of a multi-regime architecture operating over a common substrate.

rows.anchor: P(p)=0.7 ... It could represent: probability of truth; confidence in an observation; reliability of a source; posterior probability; frequency in a population; degree of belief; probability of an answer. These are mathematically different quantities. 0.7 alone has no epistemic semantics.
rows.statement: Argues a bare numeric uncertainty value (e.g. P(p)=0.7) has no epistemic semantics on its own, since it could denote any of at least 7 mathematically distinct quantities (probability of truth, observation confidence, source reliability, posterior probability, population frequency, degree of belief, or probability of an answer) -- reinforcing an earlier corpus warning against identifying measurement/probability with knowledge itself.

rows.anchor: P_M(p|E) has a meaningful interpretation relative to M. This is fundamentally different from asserting p=0.7. ... K --probabilistic regime--> D ... A probability distribution may be a regime-specific representation over a knowledge-state space [not] KnowledgeOS = Probability Distribution. The latter
rows.statement: Relocates probability from being a property directly assigned to a proposition (p=0.7) to a projection K --regime--> D produced by an explicit probabilistic model M (P_M(p|E)); explicitly rejects the earlier corpus formulation 'KnowledgeOS = Application + Distribution + Measure' as a category error, preserving instead the weaker claim that a probability distribution may be one regime-specific representation over the knowledge-state space.

rows.anchor: not every numerical assignment licenses arithmetic operations ... c(p)+c(q) is not automatically meaningful. Nor is 2c(p). Numeric representation != quantitative measurement.
rows.statement: Invokes a Roberts-style measurement-theory constraint: a numerical assignment is meaningful only when its empirical relational structure and representation theorem justify it, so arithmetic operations on a stored confidence/uncertainty number (e.g. c(p)+c(q), 2*c(p)) are not automatically meaningful -- numeric representation is not the same as quantitative measurement, a constraint relevant to any future statistical regime.

rows.anchor: Knowledge Substrate plus Semantic Relations plus Epistemic Qualifications plus Regime Specific Projections rather than one homogeneous mathematical object containing every possible quantity. ... Projection_R: K x R -> Y_R where K = knowledge substrate; R = regime; Y_R = regime-specific representatio
rows.statement: Converges on a 4-part architectural decomposition (Knowledge Substrate, Semantic Relations, Epistemic Qualifications, Regime-Specific Projections) rather than one homogeneous state object, formalized as a candidate interface Projection_R: K x R -> Y_R (K=substrate, R=regime, Y_R=regime output), instantiated for logical (LogicalModel), probabilistic (Distribution), measurement (MeasurementSpace) and governance (Decision/ComplianceAssessment) regimes -- explicitly not yet the final architecture but a testable interface.

rows.anchor: A regime may transform or interpret a knowledge substrate, but it must not silently change the historical identity of the underlying knowledge objects. ... the projection should preserve the identity mapping id_K: K -> K. A regime-specific representation must not silently turn e1 into e2.
rows.statement: States a candidate cross-regime invariant: any regime projection Pi_R(K)=Y_R must preserve the identity mapping id_K:K->K on the underlying knowledge objects -- a regime interpretation must never silently substitute one evidence/knowledge object's identity for another's, which is particularly important for provenance.
invariants: Pi_R(K)=Y_R must preserve id_K: K -> K

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS must distinguish the epistemic substrate from the mathematical regimes used to interpret it. ... Probability != Knowledge. Measurement != Knowledge. Logical inference != Knowledge. but all may operate on knowledge under properly defined regimes.
rows.statement: States the step's central principle: KnowledgeOS must distinguish the epistemic substrate from the mathematical regimes (logical, probabilistic, measurement) used to interpret it -- Probability != Knowledge, Measurement != Knowledge, Logical inference != Knowledge, though all may legitimately operate on knowledge as regimes; noted as independently arrived at, matching an existing corpus warning against equating the epistemic core with measure theory.

rows.anchor: Is the candidate Knowledge State actually a state, or is it fundamentally a history/process? ... We therefore need to test K_t versus H_t=(K_0,T_1,T_2,...,T_t) and determine whether K_t is sufficient to reconstruct everything that KnowledgeOS claims to preserve. ... the true formal object may be clo
rows.statement: Sets up the next test (named Step 247, State vs. History Sufficiency Test): whether the candidate Knowledge State K_t is sufficient by itself, or whether the true formal object must be a state-history pair (K_t, H_t) with H_t=(K0,T1,...,Tt), given the corpus's repeated emphasis on provenance/transformation/history as central rather than a single lineage component.

lineage_claims.quote: That will be the subject of Step 247 -- State vs. History Sufficiency Test.

rows.anchor: Can two knowledge states be identical while having different histories? If yes, then History(K) != K may be fundamental. Construct an example K1 and K2 with identical current semantic content but different histories. Then test K1=K2 under: structural, semantic, provenance-sensitive, historical ident
rows.statement: Mandates testing whether lambda (lineage) belongs inside K, outside K, or as a derived function History:K->Histories, via a required counterexample construction: two states with identical current semantic content but different histories, tested against 4 equality notions (structural, semantic, provenance-sensitive, historical identity) to determine whether History(K) != K is fundamental.

rows.anchor: K1 and K2 with identical content, status, temporality and policy -- differing only in history ... structural: False, semantic: True, provenance-sensitive: False, historical identity: False. ... History(K) != K is fundamental. lambda belongs OUTSIDE K, as History: K -> Histories.
rows.statement: Constructs two states K1/K2 identical in content/status/temporality/policy but differing in history, computing all four equality relations from the earlier stress test (structural=False, semantic=True, provenance-sensitive=False, historical identity=False), demonstrating semantic equality can be TRUE while historical identity is FALSE -- proving a single tuple containing lambda cannot express both relations at once, and that including lambda in K makes structural equality history-sensitive, breaking deduplication and merge. Verdict: History(K)!=K is fundamental; lambda belongs outside K as History:K->Histories, mathematically verified, and aligned with the real implementation (a separate lineage graph, no KnowledgeState).

lineage_claims.quote: This confirms Step 245's own [01] -- the open question resolves against inclusion.

rows.anchor: The equality blocker DISSOLVES once the assertion layer is restored. It was unsolvable at the level of K alone because identity lives one level down. [equality table: proposition identity, assertion identity, assertion structural/semantic equality, knowledge-state equality, historical identity -- al
rows.statement: Resolves the equality blocker (open since S1601/S1603) by showing all 6 candidate equality relations (proposition identity, assertion identity via id, assertion structural equality, assertion semantic equality ignoring evidence ids, pointwise knowledge-state equality, and historical identity as a distinct 6th relation via History(K1)=History(K2)) become computable once identity and equality are defined at the assertion level rather than forced onto K directly.

rows.anchor: I proposed a four-state set (Unknown/Supported/Refuted/Conflicted). That is one too many. Conflicted(A,K) := exists A' in K: same (subject,predicate), different object, overlapping validity, same context, neither Refuted. Conflicted is computable from the state. No operation requires it as a stored
rows.statement: Corrects a previously proposed 4-state Sigma set (adding Conflicted) down to a minimal 3-state Sigma={Unknown, Supported, Refuted}, by giving an explicit computable definition of Conflicted(A,K) as a derived predicate over the state (same subject/predicate, differing object, overlapping validity, same context, neither Refuted) that no operation requires as a stored primitive, and warning that storing it duplicates derivable information and risks an update anomaly (stored flag disagreeing with computed value).
invariants: Supported required by every other operation

rows.anchor: Two histories have the same proposition but different validity intervals theta_A(p)=[t0,t1), theta_B(p)=[t1,t2). Suppose a transformation asks CurrentVersion(S,t1+epsilon)? Then the two states produce different results. ... Temporal validity is not merely decorative metadata if temporal queries are
rows.statement: Shows via a temporal-query counterexample (CurrentVersion(S,t1+epsilon)?) that a state representation omitting temporal qualification fails congruence when temporal queries are valid operations -- confirming temporal validity is functionally load-bearing, not decorative metadata.

rows.anchor: H ~ mu_H. Then K=F(H) induces a push-forward distribution mu_K = F_* mu_H. ... mu_K is a regime-level object, not necessarily part of K.
rows.statement: Connects the state abstraction to measure theory without making it foundational: if H is a random history with distribution mu_H, then K=F(H) induces a push-forward distribution mu_K=F_*mu_H (mu_K(A)=mu_H(F^{-1}(A)) for measurable A); explicitly classifies mu_K as a regime-level object, consistent with the parallel Step 246 finding (S1601) that probability belongs to a regime projection, not to K itself.

rows.anchor: Suppose the current content is identical: Content(K1)=Content(K'1). ... e_A != e_B. And therefore H_A != H_B. ... If provenance is semantically relevant: K1 != K'1. If provenance is merely explanatory metadata: K1 = K'1. We cannot choose between them by mathematical elegance. ... History essentialit
rows.statement: Constructs a counterexample (two histories with different supporting evidence e_A!=e_B but identical resulting content) leaving whether the two resulting states should be considered equal genuinely unresolved: it depends on whether provenance is semantically constitutive (states differ) or merely explanatory metadata (states are equal) -- explicitly stating this cannot be decided by mathematical elegance alone and remains open.

rows.anchor: If H_t = f(lambda_t), then history may not need to be a separate primitive. Instead: Lineage could be a sufficient compressed representation of history. ... (K_t,H_t) is unnecessary if K_t=(Content_t,lambda_t,...) already contains all semantically relevant historical information.
rows.statement: Proposes the lineage-as-sufficient-compression hypothesis: if the full history H_t can be reconstructed from the lineage component lambda_t alone (H_t=f(lambda_t)), then the state-history pair (K_t,H_t) collapses back to a single sufficient state K_t=(Content_t,lambda_t,...), making lineage an important candidate compression of history rather than a separate primitive.

rows.anchor: History H --F--> Knowledge State K --Projection_R--> Regime Representation Y_R. ... This integrates the distribution-theoretic material without making probability part of the fundamental kernel.
rows.statement: Proposes a 3-level candidate architecture H --F--> K --Projection_R--> Y_R (history, then abstracted state, then a regime-specific representation such as logic, probability, measurement, or governance), extending the Step-246 (S1601) Projection_R interface by placing it explicitly downstream of the history-to-state abstraction F.

rows.anchor: The earlier proposal (Omega,F,mu) can now be interpreted as a regime over the state space. For example Omega=K could be a space of possible knowledge states. ... neither requires mu in K. This is a cleaner mathematical architecture.
rows.statement: Reinterprets the corpus's earlier (Omega,F,mu) measure-theoretic proposal as a probabilistic regime layered over the state space (e.g. Omega=K, the space of possible knowledge states) rather than as part of K itself -- consistent with and reinforcing the parallel Step 246/248 relocation of probability out of the kernel.

rows.anchor: Reject any numerical uncertainty claim that lacks a valid statistical basis. Distinguish: epistemic uncertainty; aleatory uncertainty; missingness; non-identifiability; contradiction; ignorance/unknown. Do not let a probability number become a substitute for these distinct concepts.
rows.statement: Mandates a statistical audit rejecting any numerical uncertainty claim lacking a valid statistical basis (random variable, sample space, estimand, observation model, probability space, conditioning information, estimator, calibration semantics, uncertainty interpretation all specified), and requires distinguishing 6 named concepts (epistemic uncertainty, aleatory uncertainty, missingness, non-identifiability, contradiction, ignorance/unknown) that a bare probability number must never be allowed to substitute for.

rows.anchor: A1 = 'v=3.69', A2 = 'v=3.70'. Is A2 a supersession of A1, or an independent observation in another context? Both readings are consistent with the same two assertions. Asserted relations carry information not present in the assertions. K = Set(Assertion) is therefore INADEQUATE. Derived relations (co
rows.statement: Gives the decisive counterexample forcing an explicit relation set R into K: two assertions (v=3.69, v=3.70) are equally consistent with being a supersession or an independent observation in a different context -- the relation information is not recoverable from the assertions alone, so K=Set(Assertion) is inadequate and asserted (not merely derived) relations must be first-class, distinguishing derived relations (contradicts, equals -- computable from content) from asserted relations (supports, supersedes, derivedFrom, refines, resolves -- not computable, must be stored).

rows.anchor: order-independence: True (frozenset ...) reflexive=True symmetric=True transitive=True => GENUINE EQUIVALENCE RELATION ... membership a in K: decidable, O(1). delta(K,o): PARTIAL (rejects), DETERMINISTIC, CLOSED. ... Two equalities, both computable and both needed: structural (includes Pi) ... seman
rows.statement: Executes and proves equality on K is a genuine equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, transitive, order-independent by construction via frozensets), membership is decidable in O(1), and state transition delta(K,o) is partial (rejects invalid inputs), deterministic, and closed; confirms both structural equality (includes Pi, so provenance-differing assertions are unequal by design) and semantic equality (ignores id/e/Pi, needed for dedup/replay) are computable and both necessary -- resolving the open equality question from S1601/S1603/S1611.

rows.anchor: The word Transformation is itself overloaded. At least three meanings currently exist: Meaning 1 -- epistemic transformation (Candidate->Knowledge); Meaning 2 -- state transformation (K->K'); Meaning 3 -- representation transformation (K->Y_R) ... 'Transformation' cannot yet be a canonical ubiquitou
rows.statement: Identifies 'Transformation' as a 3-way overloaded ubiquitous-language term (epistemic transformation Candidate->Knowledge; state transformation K->K'; representation/regime transformation K->Y_R, matching the earlier Projection_R concept), warning it cannot be used canonically without qualifying which of the three is meant, until the corpus demonstrates they are genuinely one concept.

rows.anchor: Evidence=QualifiedObservation ... is CONDITIONAL not established fact [the exact qualification function is not yet defined]. ... IdentityRelation may represent identity without defining identity. Identity != merely an arbitrary Relation unless the formal theory establishes the required equivalence p
rows.statement: Downgrades three historically proposed derived-concept equations to conditional/unresolved status: Evidence=QualifiedObservation is conditional pending a defined qualification function; Identity=EntityIdentityRelation risks representing identity without defining it (a relation is not automatically the same as semantic identity, unless equivalence properties are proven); Provenance=TypedDependencyRelation remains unresolved since Step 246's (S1601) open provenance-minimality question is unresolved.

rows.anchor: Equality cannot be finalized before the ontology of K is fixed. This is a genuine dependency, not merely a missing glossary entry. ... T cannot be fully specified independently of K. This validates the dependency concern already identified in the earlier kernel analysis.
rows.statement: Explains why equality and transition could not be finalized in earlier steps: both depend fundamentally on which of the 4 candidate ontologies (set/graph/provenance-sensitive/observational) is chosen for K -- set equality, graph isomorphism, provenance-equivalence, and behavioral equivalence are each appropriate under a different ontology, so neither equality nor transition can be specified independently of that prior choice, a genuine mathematical dependency rather than a glossary gap.

rows.anchor: prod vs staging: same P, not same assertion, discriminator c -- and not a contradiction (230.9, executed). API vs changelog: discriminator Pi, e. January vs June: discriminator t. two identical records: same assertion, content-addressed id collapses them. ... same proposition != same assertion is th
rows.statement: Executes 4 concrete discriminator cases proving 'same proposition != same assertion' is a theorem (not an axiom) derivable from the Assertion tuple's structure: production-vs-staging assertions of the same proposition differ only by context c and are explicitly not a contradiction per corpus rule 230.9; API-vs-changelog differ by provenance/evidence; January-vs-June differ by temporal validity t; and two truly identical records collapse to one assertion via the content-addressed id.

rows.anchor: str is ORDINAL. No interval structure is established anywhere in 1468 files. Therefore no arithmetic on support strength is admissible -- no averaging, no summing, no weighted evidence combination, no 'confidence scores'. Only <= and order statistics. Q14 is correct to use only the partial-order rel
rows.statement: Binds a measurement-theoretic constraint (extending the Step 246/S1601 warning) on the new signed-ordinal Sigma: the strength dimension is ordinal only, with no interval structure established anywhere across a 1468-file corpus scan, so no arithmetic (averaging, summing, weighted combination, numeric confidence scores) is admissible on it -- only ordering and order statistics -- validating Q14's own use of only the partial-order relation and flagging any corpus passage that averages/sums confidence as inadmissible.

rows.anchor: We previously treated Equality_K as foundational. But operationally, Identity must first be distinguished from Equality. Two states can be equal while containing different historical identities, depending on the chosen equivalence. Identity != Equality. The theory needs both concepts, even if they e
rows.statement: States the step's fourth major finding, reordering the theory's foundational priorities: Identity must be distinguished from Equality operationally, contrary to earlier treatment of Equality_K as the sole foundational relation -- two states can be equal under a chosen equivalence while containing different historical identities, so both concepts are independently needed.
